title: Inside the 'Gate of Tears': How a Strategic Yemeni Strait Became the World Economy's Newest Threat
snippet: Houthi rebels have seized control of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait in Yemen, creating a dangerous chokehold on global energy and maritime supply chains amidst escalating regional conflict.
content:
BAB EL-MANDEB, Yemen — To visit this dusty coastal outpost on the southwestern tip of Yemen is to witness a jarring paradox. A quiet, poverty-stricken fishing village composed of weather-beaten huts sits silently against a backdrop of rugged mountains, looking out over a narrow strip of water that anchors the global economy.

This humble stretch of land shares its name with the Bab el-Mandeb Strait—traditionally known as the "Gate of Tears" for its historically treacherous navigation. Today, the 12.5-mile-wide passage linking the Red Sea to the Arabian Sea has erupted into a critical flashpoint in the expanding broader conflict involving Iran, Israel, Saudi Arabia, and the United States.

A Rapid Shift in Control

The geopolitical landscape around the strait shifted dramatically when Houthi rebels launched a swift offensive, driving out government-aligned forces and taking full control of Yemen’s Red Sea coastline. Crucially, the rebel group captured Perim Island, a strategic landmass sitting in the middle of the strait's narrowest bottleneck.

The move gives the Iranian-backed Houthis immense leverage over a maritime artery responsible for roughly 7% of global energy supplies and upwards of 15% of international shipping traffic. From Perim Island, where regional powers had previously constructed a drone airbase and airstrip, Houthi commanders boasted that simple coastal artillery units could now easily threaten passing commercial vessels.

Global Commerce in the Crosshairs

The disruption of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait carries staggering risks for international trade. Because ships must transit the strait to reach the southern entrance of the Suez Canal, any closure or threat forces cargo vessels to reroute around the southern tip of Africa. Such a detour adds up to three weeks to maritime voyages, driving up fuel costs and straining global supply chains already reeling from regional instability.

The timing of the Houthi advance is particularly precarious. With military action in the Persian Gulf threatening traffic through the Strait of Hormuz—the world's most critical energy passageway—oil-producing giants like Saudi Arabia have increasingly relied on Red Sea routes via pipelines to export crude. Houthi control of Bab el-Mandeb effectively places a chokehold on Saudi Arabia's alternative export channels.

Escalating Regional Violence

The takeover follows a complete breakdown of a 2022 ceasefire between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis. Recent Houthi missile launches targeting Saudi industrial hubs like Taif and Yanbu prompted retaliatory airstrikes across northern Yemen. Meanwhile, Washington has reiterated its security commitments to Riyadh, with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio confirming the nation's intent to uphold defense obligations.

Speaking at the United Nations General Assembly, Yemeni Vice President Abdullah Abdulkader al Alimi-Bawzer warned that Houthi control over the waterway poses a direct threat far beyond the region's borders, accusing the rebels of holding the global economy hostage.

An Uphill Battle Ahead

Military analysts warn that dislodging Houthi forces from the coast will prove extremely difficult. In securing the territory, the rebels inherited vital infrastructure, including paved highways and airfield facilities on Perim Island. Compounded by deep divisions within the Yemeni government forces and the Houthis' expanding arsenal of ballistic missiles and attack drones, restoring stability to the "Gate of Tears" remains an elusive prospect.
